abstract: Humans move in time with musical beats, yet how the brain builds the internal beat that guides movement is unknown. We recorded 4,719 neurons in six nodes of the audiomotor circuit while monkeys tapped in synchrony with auditory metronomes at different tempos. We found a clear functional dissociation in the temporal-frontal axis. Auditory cortex detected metronome clicks and contained local clocks that tiled each interstimulus interval, whereas parietal, striatal, and motor areas, most strongly the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA), generated movement-aligned neural sequences that rescaled with tempo. Only in preSMA did population activity formed a cone-shaped manifold that jointly encoded tempo in its height, the produced interval in its width, and the timing of each tap relative to the beat in its position along the trajectory. During timing errors, preSMA activity kept conical shape but drifted toward shorter or longer tempos, revealing a hierarchical neural clock for beat synchronization.
